summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “The moon is made of green cheese, so it is raining in Ecuador or it is not.” The second statement is always one of the two choices, but it does not seem connected to the first. Relevance logic asks whether an argument should count as good when its starting idea has nothing to do with its ending idea.
summaries.summary: Relevance logic is a family of non-classical logics. It was developed partly because some rules of classical logic seem to let unrelated ideas support one another. For example, a contradiction can appear to imply any statement, and a statement can appear to imply a truth that has nothing to do with it. Relevance logicians want implication to involve a genuine connection between what comes before and what comes after. One formal test is the variable sharing principle: an implication or valid argument must have at least one propositional variable in common between its starting point and its ending point. This test is only a necessary condition, not a complete answer. The entry also explains special models with worlds, unusual treatments of negation, systems for quantifiers, proof methods that record which premises are actually used, and several different relevance logics. Some versions are strong; others are weaker and can be useful for studying set theory or computer resources.
key_ideas: Some rules in ordinary classical logic allow conclusions that seem unrelated to their premises.
Relevance logicians try to prevent these apparent mistakes, called fallacies of relevance.
Variable sharing is one useful requirement, but it does not solve every problem by itself.
Different relevance logics use different rules, models, and ideas about implication.
Some systems allow a statement to be both true and false, or neither true nor false.
Relevance logic has been studied in mathematics, computer science, and theories about information.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relevance logic teaches that a correct-looking conclusion is not always supported by the reason offered. It gives philosophers and computer scientists tools for studying connections among information, proofs, rules, and resources. It also shows that there can be more than one sensible system of logic, depending on which kinds of inference we want to accept.

important_terms.definition: A kind of logic that asks whether the reasons in an argument are connected to its conclusion.
A statement used as a reason in an argument.
The statement an argument tries to support.
A formal rule saying that a reason and its result should share at least one important symbol or idea.
A rule for checking whether a conclusion really used the reasons it was given.

questions_to_think_about: Should a reason always be connected to its conclusion?
Can an argument have a true conclusion but still be a bad argument?
Why might a contradiction not prove every statement?
What information do you need before deciding that one idea supports another?

summaries.example: Consider the inference: “The moon is made of green cheese. Therefore, either it is raining in Ecuador now or it is not.” Classical logic treats this as valid because the conclusion has the form of a statement that must be true. A relevance logician objects that the premise contributes nothing to the conclusion. The issue is not simply whether the conclusion is true; it is whether the premise is genuinely used in reaching it.
summaries.summary: Relevance logic is a group of non-classical systems that challenge the idea that every classically valid inference is acceptable. Classical material implication can validate formulas in which a false antecedent supports anything, while strict implication can validate formulas in which any statement supports a tautology. Relevance logicians regard such cases as problematic because the antecedent and consequent may be unrelated. Their central aim is to require a meaningful connection between premises and conclusions. The variable sharing principle expresses one formal version of this aim: an implication cannot be proved unless its two sides share a propositional variable. Yet this principle is not sufficient, since some unwanted inferences still share variables. The entry surveys several semantic approaches. Routley–Meyer semantics evaluates formulas at worlds or situations and uses a ternary accessibility relation to represent how information connects. Other approaches use normal and non-normal worlds or four-valued semantics, where a formula may be true, false, both, or neither. Quantified relevance logics require more elaborate semantics than simple constant-domain models. Proof theory provides another perspective: relevant natural deduction records which hypotheses contribute to a result. Different systems make different choices about contraction, transitivity, contraposition, and disjunctive syllogism. These choices produce a broad family rather than one single relevance logic. Applications include relevant predication, arithmetic, deontic and modal logic, counterfactuals, naive set theory, and linear logic, where premises can represent resources that cannot simply be duplicated.
key_ideas: Relevance logics arose partly as responses to so-called paradoxes of material and strict implication, where formal validity can result without an intuitive connection.
The variable sharing principle blocks many unrelated implications, but it is only necessary; sharing a variable does not guarantee genuine relevance.
Routley–Meyer semantics uses a three-place relation among worlds or information states to model relevant implication.
Some semantics include inconsistent or non-bivalent worlds so that contradictions and tautologies do not automatically generate every implication.
Natural-deduction systems can track which hypotheses are actually used, giving proof-theoretic meaning to relevance.
The family includes systems such as E and R, weaker systems that reject contraction, and related systems such as N4, Core Logic, and Analytic Implication.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relevance logic separates truth from support. A conclusion may be true while an offered premise fails to support it, and a formally valid route may still seem defective if it ignores its assumptions. The subject therefore connects technical logic with philosophical questions about meaning, information, explanation, and responsible reasoning. Its study also shows how changing structural rules—such as whether premises may be repeated—can produce useful logics for mathematics and computation.

important_terms.definition: A non-classical family of logics designed to require a connection between premises and conclusions.
The conditional or implication connective studied in these systems; its interpretation is intended to preserve a meaningful connection between antecedent and consequent.
A formal requirement that an implication’s two sides, or an argument’s premises and conclusion, share a propositional variable.
The study of meaning and truth conditions for formulas, often by assigning them to worlds or situations.
The study of formal proofs and the rules governing how premises may be used.
A rule allowing a premise to be used more than once in a derivation.
A semantics in which formulas may be true only, false only, both, or neither.
The inference from a contradiction to any conclusion, often called explosion.

questions_to_think_about: Is variable sharing enough to capture the ordinary idea that one statement is relevant to another?
What is gained, and what is lost, when a logic rejects explosion?
Why would a proof system need to count how many times a premise is used?
Should implication and entailment be treated as the same relation, or as related but distinct?
How might logic change when formulas represent limited computational resources rather than ordinary propositions?

summaries.example: Imagine a student argues, “The cafeteria served pizza today, so either the school bus is late or it is not late.” The conclusion has to be one of two possibilities, but the pizza does not help us decide it. Classical logic may count the argument as valid because of the form of the conclusion. Relevance logic asks a different question: did the premise actually help support the conclusion?
summaries.summary: Relevance logic is a collection of non-classical logics concerned with whether an inference stays connected to its starting points. In familiar classical logic, some formulas are valid even though the antecedent seems unrelated to the consequent. For instance, a false statement can materially imply anything, and a contradiction can appear to imply every statement. Relevance logicians see these results as possible fallacies of relevance. They propose formal systems in which a premise must play a real role in supporting its conclusion. The variable sharing principle is one basic idea: an implication cannot be proved unless its two sides share at least one propositional variable. However, sharing is only a requirement, not a full definition of relevance. The entry describes semantics that evaluate statements at worlds, situations, or information states. The Routley–Meyer approach uses a three-place relation to represent how information is connected. Other approaches use non-normal worlds or four possible truth statuses: true, false, both, or neither. Quantifiers such as “all” need especially careful treatment because ordinary classical translations can be too weak or too strong. Proof theory gives a complementary approach by recording which assumptions a proof actually uses. The field contains several systems, including the important systems E and R, weaker systems that reject contraction, and related systems with different rules. Relevance logic has also been applied to set theory, arithmetic, duties, properties, counterfactuals, and computer science. Linear logic is especially close in spirit because it treats assumptions as resources that may not be freely copied or discarded.
key_ideas: Relevance logic questions some classical inferences because their premises and conclusions may concern completely different topics.
The variable sharing principle helps keep an implication on topic, but it does not remove every questionable inference.
Some relevance models use three-place relations among worlds to represent how information in one situation connects information in another.
Non-normal or inconsistent worlds help these systems avoid treating every contradiction or logical truth as automatically relevant to everything.
Relevant proof systems can mark which assumptions were genuinely used, rather than merely listing all available assumptions.
There is no single final relevance logic: systems differ over rules such as contraction, transitivity, and disjunctive syllogism.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relevance logic helps explain why “valid” and “persuasive” are not always the same. It gives a precise way to study whether evidence contributes to a conclusion instead of merely accompanying it. Its different systems also show how small changes in rules can affect mathematics, computer reasoning, and the way information is modeled.

important_terms.definition: A family of logics that requires a real connection between an argument’s reasons and its conclusion.
The first part of an if–then statement, usually the condition or reason.
The second part of an if–then statement, usually what is said to follow.
A rule requiring the two sides of an implication to share a propositional variable.
A description of what makes a formula true in a model, such as a world or information situation.
A system of rules for building and checking formal arguments.
The rule that a contradiction can be used to derive any statement.
A logic in which a statement can be true, false, both, or neither.

questions_to_think_about: Is an argument acceptable if its conclusion is true but its premise is unrelated?
Why might a relevance logician reject the inference from a contradiction to any conclusion?
Can two formulas share a symbol without being meaningfully connected?
What might be a good reason for allowing a premise to be used only once?
How could a logic designed for information differ from one designed for ordinary statements?
